218.title: Om tat sat: the threefold name
218.hook: the three words that hand an act to God
218.carry: om tat sat: every act offered to god
218.howItsDone: Some Hindus say 'om tat sat' at the close of a reading, a ritual or a teaching; some printed Gitas set the three words in each chapter's closing line, and verse 17.24 says Vedic rites begin with om.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vidura's humble meal and sattvic food, offered with love. Today, three words that close the chapter.

In the palace at Hastinapura, the blind king Dhritarashtra sits and listens. His minister Sanjaya has been granted far sight; he can see the battlefield, and he tells the king every word spoken in Arjuna's chariot. He's heard Krishna sort food, worship and giving into three kinds. Now, at the very end of chapter seventeen, Krishna gives three words, not for sorting, but for offering. Om. Tat. Sat. You've met the first one already. It was your second word, back in camp one.
screen: `A BLIND KING LISTENS.` → `SANJAYA SEES THE CHARIOT.` → `THREE WORDS TO OFFER AN ACT.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-three. Om tat sat: this is remembered as the threefold name of Brahman, the ultimate. By it, long ago, the priests, the Vedas and the sacrifices were set in order. Then Krishna explains each word. Om first. Verse twenty-four: those who follow the Veda always begin their acts of sacrifice, giving and discipline by saying om. The sound goes first. Tat means that. Verse twenty-five: with tat, people seeking freedom do their sacrifice, discipline and giving without aiming at the reward. It's a way of saying, this isn't for me; it's for that. And sat means real, true, good. Verse twenty-six: sat is used for what is real and what is good, and for any praiseworthy act. Verse twenty-seven: steadiness in sacrifice, discipline and giving is called sat, and so is any action done for its sake. So the three words make a small arc. Om: begin with the sacred sound. Tat: offer it to that, not to yourself. Sat: let it be real and good. The chapter's last verse, twenty-eight, ties it back to faith. Whatever is offered, given or practiced without faith is called asat, unreal. It counts for nothing, here or after. The Sanskrit prefix a means not, so asat is simply not-sat. That's the teaching under the three words: in Hinduism, an act can be offered to God, begun with the sacred sound and given away before it's even done. It's why many Hindus say om before a prayer or a reading, and why some close a reading or a puja with om tat sat, handing it back.
screen: `THE THREEFOLD NAME.` · `OM: BEGIN WITH THE SOUND.` · `TAT: FOR THAT, NOT FOR ME.` · `SAT: REAL AND GOOD.` · then, large: `OM TAT SAT: OFFERED TO GOD.`

segments.voice: Think of one ordinary thing you'll do after this: cooking, a call, a task at work. If you pray, offer it the way the verses do: say om softly, the beginning; then tat, this is for you, not for me; then sat, may it be real and good. If you don't pray, take three breaths with those three thoughts. Then just sit, and let the action wait.
Sat, the real, the good. Gita seventeen, twenty-three: the threefold name of the ultimate, om tat sat; om is the sacred sound, tat is that, and sat is the real and good.
Your line: om tat sat, every act offered to God. Begin with om, give it to that, let it be sat. Tomorrow, the Gita's last chapter.

219.title: Two kinds of giving up
219.hook: Arjuna's last question: is the holy life walking away, or letting go inside?
219.carry: tyaga: let go of the fruit, not the act
219.howItsDone: Hindu tradition honors sannyasis, renunciants who leave household life, and it also teaches householders the Gita's tyaga: doing one's duties fully while letting go of attachment to results.

segments.voice: Yesterday, om tat sat: the threefold name, every act offered to God. Today, the Gita's last chapter, the graduation chapter.

Go back to the very start of the Gita. The conch shells have sounded, the armies are drawn up, and Arjuna looks across at his grandfather and his teacher. His bow slips from his hand. He sinks down in the chariot, and soon he's saying he'd rather live by begging than fight. India has an honored path that looks a little like that: the sannyasi, who leaves home, wears saffron and lives on what's given. Seventeen chapters later, Arjuna asks his last question in the whole Gita, and it goes straight back to that moment: what does it really mean to give things up?
screen: `HIS BOW SLIPS.` → `BETTER TO BEG THAN FIGHT?` → `ARJUNA'S LAST QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Verse one: Arjuna asks to know the truth of two words. Sannyasa, renunciation, and tyaga, relinquishment. Both mean giving up. Verse two: the wise say sannyasa is giving up actions done out of desire. And tyaga, they say, is giving up the fruit of all actions. Verse three admits the wise disagree. Then Krishna gives his own view, verse five: sacrifice, giving and discipline should not be abandoned. They should be done. They purify the wise. Verse six: but even these should be done without attachment, and without clinging to the fruit. This is my firm conclusion. Then the three threads come back, now applied to giving up. Verse seven: quitting your proper duty out of confusion is tamasic. Verse eight: quitting because it's hard, or you're afraid of the strain, is rajasic, and it gets you nothing. Verse nine: doing your duty because it should be done, while letting go of attachment and the fruit, that's sattvic relinquishment. Verse eleven says it plainly. No one with a body can give up action completely. But the one who gives up the fruit of action is called a relinquisher. So the Gita's answer to the man who wanted to throw down his bow is not walk away. It's stay, act, and let go of the outcome. This is karma yoga, the Gita's path of action, in its final form. Hinduism honors the monk who leaves home, and it also says a parent, a student or a worker can truly give things up without leaving, by letting go of the fruit.
screen: `SANNYASA AND TYAGA.` · `DON'T DROP THE GOOD WORK.` · `QUITTING FROM FEAR GETS NOTHING.` · `NO ONE CAN STOP ACTING.` · then, large: `TYAGA: LET GO OF THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Think of one duty you'd love to quit, something that's yours to do but heavy, and notice whether the urge to drop it is confusion or fear of the strain. Then, without deciding anything, picture doing it tomorrow, fully, but without needing it to turn out a particular way. Feel the difference in your shoulders; that's relinquishment.
Tyaga, relinquishment, letting go. Gita eighteen: sannyasa gives up actions; tyaga gives up the fruit, and Krishna's firm conclusion is to keep acting and let go of the fruit.
Your line: tyaga, let go of the fruit, not the act. Stay on the field, and loosen the grip. Two hundred nineteen days, and counting.

220.title: Five causes of every act
220.hook: Krishna counts five causes behind every act, and the doer is only one
220.carry: the doer is one cause of five
220.tomorrow: Three kinds of seeing and doing
220.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use Gita 18.13–18.16 to loosen the sense of being the sole doer, so that success doesn't feed pride and failure doesn't crush; some devotees offer the results of their actions to God for the same reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tyaga: keep acting, and let go of the fruit. Today, who actually does the acting?

Back in chapter eleven, Krishna showed Arjuna his cosmic form. Inside it, Arjuna saw the great warriors of both armies rushing in, like rivers rushing to the sea. Then Krishna told him: they are already slain by me. Be only the instrument, Arjuna. Until then, Arjuna had talked as if the whole war hung on him alone: my bow, my sin, my choice. Now, in the last chapter, Krishna takes any action at all, good or bad, and counts its causes. He finds five. And the doer is only one.
screen: `THE COSMIC FORM.` → `BE ONLY THE INSTRUMENT.` → `FIVE CAUSES FOR EVERY ACT.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen: learn from me the five causes for the completion of every action, as taught in the Samkhya teaching. Verse fourteen lists them. First, adhishthana, the seat: the body, the base where the action happens. Second, karta, the doer: the one who says I'm doing this. Third, the various instruments: the senses and the mind. Fourth, the many different efforts: the movements, the breaths, the energies that carry the action out. And fifth, daiva. Daiva is hard to translate. It can mean the divine, providence, or what some call fate or luck: the part beyond your control. Different teachers read it differently, some as God's hand, some as the weight of past karma. Verse fifteen: whatever action a person begins with body, speech or mind, right or wrong, these five are its causes. Verse sixteen is the turn. The one who sees themselves as the only doer, because their understanding is untrained, doesn't see. The doer is one cause among five. Some teachers say this cuts two ways. When things go well, it takes the air out of pride: you had help, from your body, your senses, your effort, and something beyond all of them. When things go badly, it takes some weight off guilt: not everything was yours to control. This is the root of a very Hindu habit: offering the results of what you do to God. Some devotees say sarvam Krishnarpanam, all of it offered to Krishna, when a task is done.

segments.voice: Take one breath as an action and notice the five: the seat, your body sitting; the doer, the sense that I am breathing; the instruments, nose, lungs, attention; the effort, muscles moving, air flowing. And the fifth, the part you didn't make and can't explain: that there is air, and that you're alive to breathe it. Let the breath keep going on its own.

Daiva, the divine, providence or fate. Gita eighteen, fourteen: the fifth of five causes of action, the seat, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and daiva, the unseen fifth. The doer is only one of five.
Your line: the doer is one cause of five. Not I alone, so the result can be offered. That's two hundred twenty.

221.title: Three kinds of seeing and doing
221.hook: the three gunas shape how you see, how you act and who you are while doing it
221.carry: the three gunas color how you see and act
221.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use Gita 18.19–18.28 as a mirror for work and study: aiming for sattvic knowledge, action and doing, steady, unattached and unshaken by success or failure.

segments.voice: Yesterday, daiva: five causes of action, and the doer is only one. Now the three threads, the gunas, one more time.
screen: `THE DOER IS ONE CAUSE OF FIVE.`

segments.voice: On the first morning, Arjuna asked Krishna to drive the chariot between the two armies, so he could see who he'd be fighting. He looked across and saw them one by one: grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, friends. Each face belonged to a side, mine or theirs. That's when he fell apart. For seventeen chapters, Krishna has been teaching him another way to see. Today, in chapter eighteen, he sorts seeing itself, then doing, then the doer, by the three gunas, the threads of nature.
screen: `DRIVE ME BETWEEN THE ARMIES.` → `MINE OR THEIRS.` → `THREE WAYS OF SEEING.`

segments.voice: Knowledge first. Verse twenty: sattvic knowledge sees one undying reality in all beings, undivided in the divided. It's chapter thirteen's one light, the seeing Arjuna lacked on that first morning. Verse twenty-one: rajasic knowledge sees all beings as separate, each its own thing, nothing connecting them. Verse twenty-two: tamasic knowledge clings to one small piece as if it were everything, without reason, without grasping what's true. Then action. Verse twenty-three: sattvic action is what needs doing, done without attachment, without craving or hate, by someone not chasing the fruit. Verse twenty-four: rajasic action is driven by desire or ego, done with enormous strain. Verse twenty-five: tamasic action starts in confusion, with no thought for the consequences or the harm to others. Then the doer. Verse twenty-six: the sattvic doer is free of attachment, doesn't talk about themselves, is full of steadiness and energy, and unchanged by success or failure. Verse twenty-seven: the rajasic doer is passionate, wants the fruit, is greedy, can be harmful, and swings between joy and grief. Verse twenty-eight: the tamasic doer is unsteady, stubborn, lazy, gloomy, and dirghasutri. That last word is a compound of dirgha, long, and sutra, thread. Long-threaded: someone who keeps stretching a job out. A procrastinator, sitting right there in the Gita's last chapter. The chapter goes on to sort understanding, resolve and happiness the same way. This is the Hindu teaching of the gunas: sattva, clear; rajas, restless; tamas, heavy. Every person has all three, and they shift. As many teachers read it, the point isn't to label yourself. It's to notice which thread is pulling now, and lean toward sattva.
screen: `SEEING ONE, SEEING MANY, SEEING A BIT.` · `STEADY, STRAINED, OR CARELESS.` · `THE DOER UNCHANGED BY SUCCESS.` · `DIRGHASUTRI: THE PROCRASTINATOR.` · then, large: `THREE GUNAS, THREE WAYS TO SEE.`

segments.voice: Think of one task waiting for you, and notice, without judgment, how you're seeing it: part of something bigger, only your piece, or one annoying detail? Notice, too, how you'd do it: steadily, frantically, or not at all yet. Then picture doing it the steady way, with energy but without needing praise, and hold that picture for a few breaths.

Dirghasutri, long-threaded, one who drags a task out. Gita eighteen, nineteen to twenty-eight: knowledge, action and the doer each come in three kinds, sattvic, rajasic and tamasic, and the tamasic doer is dirghasutri.
Your line: the three gunas color how you see and act. Notice the thread, then lean toward sattva. On to day two hundred twenty-two tomorrow.

222.title: Your own dharma
222.hook: your own path, done badly, beats someone else's done well
222.carry: svadharma: your own dharma, even imperfect
222.howItsDone: Some Hindus understand svadharma as the duties that belong to their own life and stage of life, and offer their daily work as worship; how the Gita's varna verses relate to birth-based caste is still debated among Hindus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three gunas, and dirghasutri, the long-threaded procrastinator. Today, a hard and important passage.

Remember what Arjuna said in chapter two, slumped in the chariot? Better to live by begging, like a holy man, than to kill his own teachers. He was reaching for someone else's life, one that looked purer than the life in front of him. Krishna answered in chapter three with a line he now repeats in chapter eighteen, almost word for word: your own dharma, even done imperfectly, is better than someone else's, done well. But the verses around it need care.
screen: `BETTER TO BEG THAN FIGHT?` → `SOMEONE ELSE'S LIFE.` → `YOUR OWN, EVEN IMPERFECT.`

segments.voice: Verses forty-one to forty-four describe the four varnas, the classes of ancient Indian society: brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras. Their work, Krishna says, is divided by the qualities born of their nature. Calm, self-control, learning and faith for brahmins. Courage, skill and generosity for kshatriyas, Arjuna's class of warriors. Farming, cattle and trade for vaishyas. Service for shudras. This is where honesty matters. You met a classmate's version of this question on day ninety-five; here it is in the Gita itself. These verses have been used to support caste as a hierarchy fixed by birth, and people were deeply hurt by it. The reformer B. R. Ambedkar criticized the Gita sharply for this. Some modern Hindu teachers read varna as temperament and calling rather than birth, pointing to chapter four, where Krishna says the four were made by quality and action. Hindus still disagree about this, and the disagreement is real. Then verse forty-five turns to the heart of the passage: a person who is devoted to their own work reaches perfection. Verse forty-six: by worshiping, through their own work, the one from whom all beings come, a person reaches perfection. In this verse, work itself becomes worship. Verse forty-seven: better your own dharma, even imperfect, than another's, even done well. Verse forty-eight adds: don't abandon the work that's yours, even if it has flaws. Every undertaking is wrapped in some fault, the way fire is wrapped in smoke. Whatever one makes of the varna verses, these last four teach svadharma: each life has its own right work, and doing it, smoke and all, can be worship.
screen: `FOUR VARNAS, BY QUALITY AND WORK.` · `USED TO DEFEND CASTE BY BIRTH.` · `YOUR WORK CAN BE WORSHIP.` · `EVERY FIRE HAS SOME SMOKE.` · then, large: `SVADHARMA: YOUR OWN DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Think of a life you've envied lately, let it come fully into view, then gently set it down. Now think of the work actually in front of you, your family, your work, your studies, and notice its imperfections, the smoke. Then notice the fire, the part that's truly yours, that no one else could do quite the same way. If you pray, offer the next hour of it to God, as verse forty-six describes; if you don't, give it your full attention, and rest there.

223.title: The road to Brahman
223.hook: Krishna draws the whole road to Brahman, and finds love at the top
223.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers read Gita 18.49–18.58 as a summary of the whole spiritual path, from unattached work and disciplined living to realizing Brahman and supreme devotion (para bhakti).

segments.voice: Yesterday, svadharma: your own dharma, even imperfect, and every fire has some smoke. Today, where that road leads.

Picture the scene the blind king is hearing about. Two armies have stood on the field at Kurukshetra this whole time, conches blown, bows raised, waiting, while a charioteer and a prince talk between the lines. Seventeen chapters of questions. Now Krishna does what a guide does near the end of a long climb: he stops and draws the whole road at once. In about ten verses it runs from ordinary work, done without clinging, all the way to Brahman, the ultimate reality. And at the top, there's a surprise.
screen: `TWO ARMIES, WAITING.` → `THE WHOLE ROAD AT ONCE.` → `A SURPRISE AT THE TOP.`

segments.voice: Verse forty-nine: with understanding unattached everywhere, self mastered, desire gone, a person reaches through relinquishment the highest perfection, freedom from the bind of action. Verse fifty: now hear, briefly, how the one who's reached that perfection reaches Brahman. Then the road, verses fifty-one to fifty-three. A clear understanding. Holding yourself steady with resolve. Setting aside sound and the other sense objects, putting down liking and disliking. Seeking quiet, solitary places, eating lightly, speech, body and mind held in check. Always turning to meditation, resting in dispassion. Letting go of ego, force, pride, desire, anger, and the need to own things. Free of mine, at peace. That one, Krishna says, is fit to become Brahman. The word that holds it together is dhriti, steadiness, resolve. Not a burst of effort. A steady hand. Then verse fifty-four, the summit, and a surprise. Having become Brahman, serene, that person neither grieves nor craves. The same toward all beings, they reach the highest love for me. One might expect the road to end in a merging where love disappears. Here, on becoming Brahman, love begins. Verse fifty-five: by love they know me as I truly am, and knowing me, they enter me. Advaita teachers read this as knowledge completing itself; Vaishnava teachers read it as devotion as the goal. Both keep the verse, and in its own words the summit isn't a blank: it's love. Then Krishna turns to Arjuna. Verse fifty-seven: give all your actions to me in your mind. Verse fifty-eight: with your mind on me, by my grace you'll cross every obstacle. But if, out of ego, you won't listen, you'll be lost.
screen: `PERFECTION THROUGH LETTING GO.` · `STEADY: SIMPLE, QUIET, FREE OF MINE.` · `BECOMING BRAHMAN, LOVE BEGINS.` · `BY MY GRACE YOU'LL CROSS.` · then, large: `THE ROAD TO BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Try one piece of the road, steadiness: spine upright, breath even. When a sound comes, let it pass without liking or disliking it; when a thought of mine comes, my plans, my things, let it pass too. Don't force anything; just hold steady, like a hand around a cup of water, firm but not tight.
Brahmabhuta, having become Brahman. Gita eighteen, forty-nine to fifty-eight: relinquishment, steadiness, a quiet, solitary life free of mine, becoming Brahman, and then the highest love.
Your line: becoming Brahman, love begins. Steady on the road, and love at the summit. See you tomorrow.

224.title: Do as you choose
224.hook: after seven hundred verses, Krishna hands the decision back to Arjuna
224.carry: god teaches, then trusts you to choose
224.tomorrow: "Abandon all dharmas, come to me alone" (18.66–18.72)
224.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often point to Gita 18.63, 'reflect fully, then do as you wish', as a sign that the Gita invites understanding and free choice rather than blind obedience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, brahmabhuta: the whole road to Brahman. Your line was becoming Brahman, love begins. Today, the most surprising move in the book.

Think of everything Arjuna has been given on that chariot. Seventeen chapters of answers. Once, a vision of Krishna's universal form so overwhelming that he begged to see the gentle form again. Out on the field, the armies are still waiting for one man to lift his bow or lay it down. Now, at the very end, Krishna could simply say: fight. Instead, he closes the teaching and hands the decision back.
screen: `SEVENTEEN CHAPTERS OF ANSWERS.` → `ONE OVERWHELMING VISION.` → `THEN: DO AS YOU CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: It starts with a warning. Verse fifty-nine: if, leaning on your ego, you think, I will not fight, that decision is useless. Your own nature will push you to it. Verse sixty: bound by your own work, born of your nature, you'll do helplessly what you, confused, don't want to do. Then verse sixty-one, a strange picture: the Lord lives in the heart of every being, Arjuna, and by his power moves them all, as if they were mounted on a machine. Verse sixty-two: go to him for refuge with your whole being; by his grace you'll reach the highest peace. Then verse sixty-three. I have told you this wisdom, more secret than any secret. Reflect on it fully. Then do as you wish. Yathecchasi tatha kuru. As you wish, so do. After all the teaching, all the argument, the vision of chapter eleven, Krishna doesn't force a choice. The Gita's God persuades, shows, loves, and then respects Arjuna enough to let him decide. But he doesn't walk away. Verse sixty-four: hear my highest word once more. You are deeply loved by me. Verse sixty-five repeats a line from chapter nine: keep your mind on me, be devoted to me, and you will come to me. I promise you truly, for you are dear to me. So the handing back isn't cold. It comes wrapped in the plainest statement of love in the whole book. Many teachers see a deep Hindu idea here: the Lord lives in every heart, and still the choice is put in human hands. And it closes the week: om tat sat, letting go of the fruit, five causes, the gunas, your own dharma, the road to Brahman, and now this.
screen: `YOUR NATURE WILL MOVE YOU.` · `THE LORD IN EVERY HEART.` · `REFLECT, THEN DO AS YOU WISH.` · `YOU ARE DEEPLY LOVED.` · then, large: `NOW DO AS YOU CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one choice you're facing. If you pray, bring it to God first, as verse sixty-two invites. Let all the advice you've been given about it, from people, from books, from these days, be said once; then let it go quiet. In the quiet, reflect on it fully, the way verse sixty-three asks. You don't have to decide; just notice that the choice is yours, and that you can make it without fear.
Yathecchasi, as you wish. Gita eighteen, sixty-three: after all the teaching, Krishna says reflect fully, then do as you wish, yathecchasi tatha kuru.
Your line: God teaches, then trusts you to choose. And you are deeply loved. That's day two hundred twenty-four.
